title: Closing the AI accountability gap: defining an end-to-end framework for internal algorithmic auditing
journal: Proceedings of the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency
abstract: Rising concern for the societal implications of artificial intelligence systems has inspired a wave of academic and journalistic literature in which deployed systems are audited for harm by investigators from outside the organizations deploying the algorithms. However, it remains challenging for practitioners to identify the harmful repercussions of their own systems prior to deployment, and, once deployed, emergent issues can become difficult or impossible to trace back to their source. In this paper, we introduce a framework for algorithmic auditing that supports artificial intelligence system development end-to-end, to be applied throughout the internal organization development life-cycle. Each stage of the audit yields a set of documents that together form an overall audit report, drawing on an organization's values or principles to assess the fit of decisions made throughout the process. The proposed auditing framework is intended to contribute to closing the accountability gap in the development and deployment of large-scale artificial intelligence systems by embedding a robust process to ensure audit integrity.
explain_beginner: AI systems are often found to cause real harm, a hiring tool that quietly favors one group, a risk score that treats people unfairly, only after they are already out in the world and someone outside the company notices. This paper argues that companies should instead audit their own AI systems for potential harm while still building them, not after the fact, and lays out a concrete five stage process for how to do it, define what the system is meant to do and who it affects, map out everyone with a stake in it, collect the paperwork that documents how it was built, actually test it against real failure cases, and reflect on what was found and what should change before release. Each stage is meant to leave behind a real document, not just a conversation. The authors are honest that this is only part of the answer, since people auditing their own company's product can never be fully independent, and the process assumes documentation habits that move much slower than typical AI development schedules.
explain_business: For any organization building AI in house, this is a template for what an internal audit trail should look like before a regulator or a lawsuit forces the question, specific documents at each build stage, ethical review, stakeholder map, datasheets, model cards, test results, and a remediation plan, rather than a single after the fact report. The practical payoff is that reconstructing this evidence after an AI system has already caused harm is far more expensive and often impossible, so the cost of building the paper trail as you go is lower than the cost of proving compliance retroactively. The catch the authors themselves flag is that internal auditors are not neutral, they work for the company whose product they are reviewing, so this process reduces but does not eliminate the case for an external, independent audit on top of it, particularly for any AI system a regulator would classify as high risk.
explain_practitioner: Raji and coauthors propose SMACTR, an internal audit lifecycle spanning Scoping, Mapping, Artifact Collection, Testing, and Reflection, each producing specific deliverables, an ethical and social impact review at scoping, a stakeholder map and design history review at mapping, datasheets and model cards as collected artifacts, adversarial test results and an ethical risk chart at testing, and a remediation plan plus audit summary report at reflection. The paper's contribution is procedural rather than empirical, it does not report a success metric on a specific benchmark, instead it formalizes a lifecycle meant to be run inside any organization building AI. The authors state their own limitation directly, internal auditors necessarily share an organizational interest with the system they are auditing, so the framework is explicitly positioned as one piece of a broader accountability system that still needs external oversight, and they flag that setting clear pass or fail thresholds during testing, such as how close a fairness metric needs to be to parity, remains genuinely unresolved.
